source.title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on feature-to-neuron alignment, feature recurrence, and capacity-limited teacher–student networks. It refines broad claims about dictionary features and superposition, including evidence that narrower students can approximate some teacher-neuron behavior without copying the corresponding weights.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results about reconstruction, attribution, interpretability, arithmetic, distress, and feature steering that do not directly test these claim versions; those are not rows here. Values used only to select thresholds, layers, or settings are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study's own results bear on V4 and V5. Many late-layer transcoder features turn out to be single neurons, not superposed directions. Most dictionary features do not recur across seeds. Non-neuron features carry little Jacobian faithfulness. Separately, a width-limited student–teacher distillation bears on V2's prioritization account: high-energy teacher neurons get dedicated student neurons, others are approximated without a weight copy. The paper argues these results restrict what dictionary features can be taken to show about superposition.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right but misses the main framing. The authors conclude that a large share of transcoder activations (about half in late layers) come from 'neuron features' that duplicate single MLP neurons. Only these features recur across seeds and carry Jacobian faithfulness. They argue MLP neurons are a stronger interpretability basis than assumed, and say their findings 'cast doubt' on resolving within-layer MLP superposition with dictionary learning. They remain unsure whether non-neuron monosemantic features (bigrams, 'red') are truly represented by the model. The toy distillation suggests narrow students prioritize high-energy neurons and may approximate others in superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares learned transcoders and sparsified neurons, and separately distills a gated-MLP teacher into gated-MLP students; it does not reproduce the original toy-model method or its feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Neuron-feature prevalence depends on model, layer, transcoder training pipeline or architecture, dictionary width, sparsity, and the cosine threshold (reported thresholds vary across transcoders). Student-teacher representation changes with student width. Bigram matching differs between plain and Matryoshka TopK training.

fits_no_version.finding: A same-width gated-MLP student copies only 72.6% of teacher neurons at threshold 0.7. An MoE transcoder with abundant width represents only 25.6% of neurons (44.0% with neuron initialization). Distillation fails to replicate teacher units even without capacity pressure.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MSE distillation into an equal-capacity student does not reliably reproduce the teacher's neuron basis.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse probing on 113 tasks: top-k sign-split neurons match or exceed transcoders on every model tested (e.g. AUC 0.854 vs 0.832 on Gemma 3 4B). Top neuron activations score comparably to transcoder features on sort evals.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparsified neurons are as interpretable as dictionary features at the top of their activation range.

record.peer_reviewed: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Workshop: Interpretability as a Science
record.problems: The authors state that the evidence is restricted mainly to base models, mostly English data, sparse high-magnitude single-token activations, per-layer dictionaries, and first-order Jacobian faithfulness. They do not provide a systematic human evaluation, and they say they are uncertain how well transcoder features decompose the model’s computation or how broadly the results generalize. The toy student–teacher experiment does not characterize the geometry of any superposed directions.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the selected versions. The paper’s many per-layer Jacobian plots, additional seed/width sweeps, and case-study feature examples were not all itemized where they did not add a distinct result for the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: All of V1. There is no sparse-feature toy model, no measurement of near-orthogonal overlap geometry, and no sparsity-dependent phase transition.
The claim that polysemanticity in neurons is caused by capacity competition. The toy experiment measures which teacher neurons a narrower student keeps, not polysemanticity.
All of V3. No test of polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
All of V6. The linebreaking manifold and tiling remarks are discussion only, with no test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Width sweep of cross-seed shared features versus neuron features, and IoU falling with width (0.74 to 0.47 for TopK k=64). In the JumpReLU pipeline, 67k stable features versus 13k neuron features at 262k width: many stable non-neuron features exist there, which softens the V5 challenge for JumpReLU.
In the TopK pipeline, non-neuron features stay near random initialization (median encoder cos to init +0.48 vs 0.03 for neuron features).

MoE transcoder: firing density predicts which neurons are represented with AUC 0.79 at baseline but only 0.63 under neuron initialization. Capacity prioritization depends on the initialization choice.
'Red' case study: TopK transcoder features combine 2–4 polysemantic neurons (OMP cos 0.85 vs 0.73 from one neuron) into monosemantic 'red' features, evidence of sparse features a dictionary recovers.
Coverage of neurons by at least one transcoder feature rises from 78% at 32k width to 93% at 256k, then plateaus.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The V2 evidence comes from a distillation of a real LLM MLP, not a sparse-feature toy model. The V4 and V5 results depend on the cosine threshold (0.6–0.9), the training pipeline (TopK vs JumpReLU) and the initialization. r27 was relinked from V4 to V5. Rows r23 and r25 are baselines and should be merged into r24 and r26.

versions.untested_parts: The toy student–teacher experiment concerns width-limited representation, but does not measure sparse-feature overlap geometry, near-orthogonality, or a sparsity-dependent transition and regular geometry.

The toy experiment tests teacher-neuron representation as student width changes and whether activation energy predicts representation. It does not test a general account of polysemanticity across networks or directly establish that every unrepresented feature shares a dimension.
The study discusses polysemantic neurons and feature clustering, but does not test whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.

Tests transcoder features’ alignment with neurons and dictionary recovery of bigram-related signals in selected LLMs. Does not establish that LLM features generally spread across many neurons, or test SAE recovery across models beyond the reported examples.
Tests recurrence across seeds for transcoders and two MLP-output SAEs. Does not establish completeness or canonicality of dictionary features.
The paper analyzes single-direction, sign-split gated-MLP neurons, but does not test whether the features that are superposed are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
